findings.quote: it wants a probe inside a machine that later burns
findings.note: class 1/4 (variety consistency): 'want' in the sense 'need/require' is labelled chiefly British; the unit is otherwise consistently American (neighbors, smolder, toward, fire department, cooperative, per square foot, grain elevator), so this is the one lexical Briticism in an AmE register. Editor's rewrite: 'it needs a probe inside a machine that later burns'.

findings.quote: The two kinds of dryer came out about equally dusty inside.
findings.note: class 1/2 (variety consistency, countability): singular count noun after plural 'kinds of' is a British pattern; American copy takes the plural. Editor's rewrite: 'The two kinds of dryers came out about equally dusty inside.'

findings.quote: her crews still take buckets of fines out of ducts in February from machines that swabbed clean in September
findings.note: class 3 (collocation/clarity): two competing source phrases stacked around a time adverbial - 'out of ducts ... from machines' - makes the reader re-parse; 'out of ducts' is redundant once 'from machines' arrives. Editor's rewrite: 'her crews still pull buckets of fines in February from machines that swabbed clean in September'.

class 3 (collocation): 'hire out' standardly means to let something out for payment (BrE) or to take employment oneself (AmE); the sense wanted here is paying someone else to do the drying. Editor's rewrite: 'rather than paying to have it done' / 'rather than having it custom-dried'.

findings.quote: Ask anyone in the county who dries grain for money which machine burns
findings.note: class 2 (clarity/structure): two wh-clauses collide at 'for money which machine burns', producing a garden path on first reading. Editor's rewrite: 'Ask any custom drier in the county which machine burns'.

findings.quote: The first summer goes on working out which to keep.
findings.note: class 3 (collocation/ambiguity): 'go on' + gerund is first read as 'continue doing'; the intended sense is the BrE 'be spent on', which normally takes a noun object ('the afternoon went on repairs'). The clash makes the reader re-parse. Editor's rewrite: 'The first summer is spent working out which to keep.'

class 3 (idiom discrimination): unlike gaps 1, 3 and 5, this gap is not carried by collocation - 'Curiously,' and 'Increasingly,' are both idiomatic English sentence adverbs in the frame, so the key 'Strictly,' is selected only by the discourse that follows ('That is the clause ... It is simply not what the list runs on'). Sound but weaker than its neighbours as an English-idiom item.

findings.quote: The can that stands a course above its neighbours
findings.note: class 3/4 (term consistency, register): the piece names the object 'pots' in the title and twice in the text, then switches without a gloss to 'can', the chiefly Scottish trade term. In a 158-word piece an editor either keeps 'pot' or glosses the switch. Editor's rewrite: 'The pot that stands a course above its neighbours'.

findings.quote: Yards sold whatever was in stock
findings.note: class 3 (clarity): 'Yards' as a bare subject on first mention is momentarily read as the unit of length or as gardens; the builders'/builder's-merchant sense is only recoverable downstream. Editor's rewrite: 'Builders' yards sold whatever was in stock'.
